---
title: "Artifact Graphs, Runtime Effects, and Operations"
unit_id: "unit-17"
---

## The Release That Succeeded Twice

The security update from the previous unit is merged. The release job invokes
the approved adapter, the command exits successfully, and the deployment log
records the new version. A second service reads the release API and confirms
success.

Production still serves the old package.

Both reports came from the same control-plane record. A downstream replication
step partially failed after the release API committed. The observer compared
the expected version with another projection of the command record rather than
with the package actually served. The rollback tool restored the control-plane
pointer but did not remove two newly written cache objects. An operator sees a
green release, a green verification, and users receiving vulnerable code.

The failure crosses three boundaries.

The artifact boundary asks which source, build, package, evidence, and release
objects are related, and how strongly. The runtime boundary asks which
authority allowed a proposal to cause which effect. The operations boundary
asks how the organization detects divergence, contains it, degrades service,
recovers, compensates, and retains custody of unknown or irreversible effects.

Artifact Graphs make provenance and replay explicit. Runtime Adapters mediate
tools, permissions, approvals, effect leases, and receipts. Governed Operations
joins expected and actual state with incident command and recovery. None makes
logs identical to reality. Their purpose is to make the gap visible and
actionable.

## Artifacts Form a Graph, Not a Folder

A repository tree shows where files are stored. An artifact graph shows how a
claim-bearing object came to exist and what depends on it.

Nodes may include requests, source snapshots, context transactions, plans,
patches, tool calls, builds, tests, proofs, reviews, packages, approvals,
deployments, observations, incidents, corrections, and publications. Edges
carry roles such as generated-from, compiled-from, tested-against, reviewed-by,
approved-for, deployed-as, observed-at, supersedes, contradicts, invalidates,
or compensates-for.

The edge role matters. A test report derived from a build is not evidence that
the build was deployed. A release page linked to a package is not proof that
the package bytes came from the reviewed source. A rollback record related to
an incident is not proof that every effect was reversed.

Each important artifact has a semantic identity and a content identity. A
semantic identity says what role the object plays: the release candidate for
job J under contract C. A content identity binds exact bytes or structured
state. Version, producer, environment, policy, source and context parents,
creation time, expiry, audience, confidentiality, and maximum inference travel
with it.

Immutable does not mean eternally correct. The original release receipt remains
in history after the deployment is found defective. A correction adds a new
node and explicit relation. Preserving the false historical record is useful
because decisions and downstream artifacts may have consumed it.

## Provenance Has Completeness Boundaries

An artifact can have flawless recorded lineage while omitting an important
parent. The build system may record source and compiler but not a fetched
dependency. The release record may bind the package digest but omit a mutable
configuration. The observer may retain a response body but not the routing
layer that selected the responding service.

Provenance therefore states its inventory. It identifies which object classes,
effects, environments, and external systems are expected to appear; how their
identities are acquired; which collectors are trusted; and which surfaces are
outside coverage.

Completeness is relative to a purpose. A graph may be complete enough to
rebuild documentation but inadequate for a security incident. It may bind
repository and package bytes while lacking the user-visible configuration.

Missingness remains first-class. Unknown parent, unavailable log, unobserved
effect, collector outage, and untracked external copy are not represented as
empty success. They change replay grade, support eligibility, recovery, and
release decisions.

Cryptographic digests make substitution detectable under their assumptions.
They do not establish that the hashed object is truthful, safe, complete, or
the one that affected the world. Signatures bind a key and message; they do
not make the key holder a legitimate authority. Attestation can narrow the
trusted base while leaving hardware, firmware, configuration, and semantic
interpretation as assumptions.

## Audit Logs Are Event Claims

An audit log is a sequence of event claims made by collectors. It is not the
world itself.

A useful event binds actor or process identity, parent job, authority, action,
target, expected effect, observed pre-state, attempted transition, observed
post-state, time basis, collector, evidence, and residuals. Append-only storage
helps reveal later alteration. Cross-signing, replication, sequence numbers,
hash chains, independent observers, and external anchors can make some forms
of omission or rewriting harder.

These mechanisms remain bounded. A compromised collector can faithfully append
a false observation. Two logs may agree because they share one upstream
source. A process can cause an uninstrumented network or physical effect. A
clock can drift. An operator can act outside the recorded tool path.

The audit design therefore includes challenge. Sample events are compared with
source systems. Independent consumers reconstruct selected decisions. Missing
sequence ranges and conflicting observations route to investigation. The
system records which claims rely on the log and what happens when its
faithfulness is disputed.

The right question is not “Do we have logs?” It is “Which consequences can be
inferred from these collectors, under what threat model, and what evidence
would reveal that the inference failed?”

## Replay Has Grades

“Reproducible” often compresses very different accomplishments.

Record replay reconstructs the sequence of declared events. Computational
replay reruns code with named inputs and environment. Artifact replay produces
the same bytes. Semantic replay produces an equivalent result for a stated
consumer. Effect replay restores or reproduces a bounded external state.
Operational replay demonstrates that the service, dependencies, monitors, and
recovery path behave as required.

These grades do not automatically imply one another. A deterministic build may
reproduce package bytes while the original deployment depended on an external
configuration. A record replay may reconstruct a release decision without
showing that production ever served the artifact. A local filesystem rollback
may be exact while an email, payment, credential disclosure, or physical action
remains irreversible.

A replay packet states target grade, source objects, environment, trusted
components, expected observations, tolerances, missingness, external effects,
and result. Partial replay can be valuable. It must not be promoted into a
stronger grade.

For the security release, byte-exact rebuild answers whether the source can
produce the package. A separate deployment replay exercises the adapter and
replication path in an isolated environment. An actual-state probe inspects the
served package. Recovery replay restores both control-plane state and cache
objects. Each result closes a different obligation.

## Runtime Adapters Are Effect Boundaries

The model or planner should propose an action. A runtime adapter interprets
that proposal against typed authority and causes the permitted effect.

An adapter invocation binds parent job, worker identity, capability, target,
arguments, impact class, authority receipt, approval if required, effect lease,
sandbox, secret handles, expected precondition, expected mutation, rollback or
compensation plan, observation method, audit destination, and expiry.

The adapter does not ask only whether the worker can call a function. It asks
whether this worker may use this capability for this job, target, purpose,
time, and effect. A general repository-write permission should not authorize
release. A valid approval for package A should not authorize package B. A
lease that expired while a plan waited should not revive because the model
still remembers it.

Least privilege applies to information and effects. Secrets remain behind
handles when possible rather than entering model-visible context. Filesystem,
network, process, repository, cloud, financial, communication, and physical
capabilities are separately scoped. High-impact or irreversible actions
require stronger approval, observation, and recovery conditions.

The adapter is a policy-enforcement point, not the entire security boundary.
The operating system, service, credential store, network, hardware, and target
API must enforce the assumptions it makes. If a tool can escape through an
unmediated path, a perfect adapter record becomes theater.

## Approval Is a Scoped Input

Human approval should be an explicit, expiring input bound to the exact action
and evidence the person reviewed.

The approval records approver identity and role, job and proposal version,
scope, target, impact, evidence refs, unresolved residuals, time, expiry,
conditions, and revocation route. A material change to arguments, artifact,
target, or risk invalidates or narrows it.

Approval does not prove comprehension, competence, independence, correctness,
or legitimacy. The interface can overload, persuade, or mislead the reviewer.
Repeated low-value prompts can create alarm fatigue. An organization can call
a click “human control” while making refusal impractical.

The runtime therefore treats approval as one authority condition, accompanied
by workload, context, independence, and consequence-sensitive controls. Safe
defaults deny or narrow when approval is missing, stale, mismatched, or
revoked. A denial should include no-mutation evidence where the system relies
on the claim that no effect occurred.

For low-consequence reversible work, pre-authorized policies can avoid constant
interruptions. Escalation is reserved for exceptions and high-impact effects.
The design objective is meaningful control, not maximum clicking.

## Effect Leases Bound Action in Time

An effect lease grants a capability under a bounded purpose, target, authority
ceiling, environment, start, expiry, and revocation policy. It can require a
fresh precondition immediately before dispatch.

Leases prevent a plan from treating old permission as permanent. They also
help partition planning from execution. The planner may prepare a release while
the lease is absent. The adapter dispatches only after current authority,
approval, and pre-state align.

Distributed systems complicate revocation. A worker may hold a stale grant
while another service records its withdrawal. If consistency cannot be
guaranteed during a partition, the system chooses an explicit policy: deny
consequential effects without fresh authority, quarantine the result, restrict
operations to a safe subset, or accept a named residual under institutional
authority.

The grant/effect race needs custody. Revocation after dispatch cannot make an
already caused effect disappear. The receipt records whether execution began,
which mutations were observed, and who owns compensation. A timeout is not
evidence of nonexecution.

## Expected Effect and Actual Effect Are Different Records

Before dispatch, the invocation declares an expected transition: package P at
version old becomes package P at version new, with named cache and registry
updates. The adapter observes pre-state, performs the attempt, and records what
it can observe afterward.

The result distinguishes command status, adapter observation, target-system
acknowledgment, independent actual-state observation, and downstream outcome.
A zero exit status belongs to the first category. It cannot stand in for the
last four.

An effect receipt binds invocation identity, exact authority and artifacts,
pre-state, attempted calls, returned statuses, observed post-state, external
effects, verification, rollback handle, incident links, and residual unknowns.
The receipt says which observer produced each field and which surfaces were
not visible.

For the release, the adapter can observe that the control plane accepted the
new package. An independent probe should inspect the package served through the
production route. The two observations may disagree. That disagreement opens
an operational decision rather than being averaged into success.

No-mutation evidence also has scope. A denied adapter call may demonstrate that
its own dispatch function did not run. It may not establish that another
worker or stale process caused no effect.

## Observation Has a Budget and a Failure Policy

Actual-state observation consumes storage, compute, network capacity, operator
attention, privacy, and time. A system cannot inspect every effect forever.
The operations contract therefore chooses sensors by consequence, uncertainty,
failure detectability, and recovery value.

Each required observation has a freshness bound, expected coverage, missing-
data behavior, calibration or challenge route, retention policy, and owner.
The system decides in advance what happens when the sensor is unavailable. A
missing post-release probe may hold a consequential rollout, reduce its cohort,
switch to an independent instrument, or enter an explicitly authorized
degraded state. It should not silently convert absence into success.

Sampling can control cost, but rare or concentrated harms need targeted
coverage. Privacy-sensitive observation may require aggregation, local
computation, strict purpose limits, or affected-party reporting rather than
more centralized telemetry. The best monitor is not always the one with the
largest data stream.

Observation policy should itself face incidents. A detector can drift, a
dashboard can omit a region, and alert thresholds can optimize for calm. The
artifact graph records detector and configuration versions so a later review
can identify which decisions depended on a defective view.

## Rollback Is an Effect Claim

Rollback should name the baseline, effect inventory, reversal method,
observation, and residuals. “Restore previous version” is inadequate when the
operation touched configuration, caches, credentials, messages, indexes,
payments, human decisions, or external services.

Some effects can be restored exactly. Some require compensation. Some can be
contained but not reversed. Some are unknown. The recovery record separates
these cases.

An exact local file restoration does not establish ACID transactions, crash
consistency, distributed recovery, or reversal of open-world effects. A
database transaction does not retract an email. Revoking a credential does
not erase a disclosed secret. Deleting an artifact does not recall every copy.

The security release's rollback inventory includes release pointer, served
package, cache objects, registry metadata, notifications, and any downstream
consumer. If two cache writes remain after the control pointer is restored,
the rollback is partial. Service may need to stay degraded until those objects
are removed or isolated.

## Change Control Joins Artifact and Authority

A change is not governed merely because its diff was reviewed. Change control
binds the proposed semantic difference, exact artifacts, affected service,
authority, evidence, rollout, observation, recovery, communication, and
expiry. It distinguishes approval to create an artifact, approval to integrate
it, and approval to expose it to an environment or public.

The record describes expected benefit and risk, dependencies, compatibility,
affected parties, rollout cohorts, canary criteria, stop thresholds, fallback,
and who may make each decision. An emergency path can be faster, but it names
which checks were deferred and creates custody for completing or compensating
them later.

Progressive delivery limits blast radius only when cohorts are meaningful and
outcomes are observed. A canary drawn from easy internal traffic may say little
about the population at risk. A feature flag can stop future access while
leaving data migrations or messages already caused. The rollout plan states
which effects are gated and which are not.

Configuration belongs to the artifact graph. A binary that passed tests can
behave differently under runtime flags, prompts, policies, model versions,
retrieval indexes, credentials, or routing rules. “No code change” is not “no
system change.” The same identity and authority discipline applies to these
mutable components.

Change windows and freeze periods are risk controls, not rituals. They are
useful when staffing, dependency stability, external events, or recovery
capacity change consequence. They should be overridden only through explicit
authority and observed conditions, not because an agent estimates that the
patch is simple.

## Incidents Begin With Divergence

An incident can begin when expected and observed state diverge, when a control
fails, when uncertainty crosses a consequence threshold, or when an affected
party reports harm. It does not require certainty about root cause.

The incident record preserves triggering observations, competing hypotheses,
scope, consequence, reversibility, propagation risk, timing, affected parties,
authority, and unknowns. Classification determines the command envelope, not
the truth of the cause.

Incident command assigns accountable roles for decision, operations,
communication, evidence, affected-party contact, and recovery. The commander
coordinates within an authority ceiling. Emergency authority is explicit,
time-bounded, logged, reviewable, and unable to erase protected constraints.

The first goal is often to prevent additional harm while preserving enough
evidence to understand what happened. That can mean revoking a lease,
quarantining an artifact, stopping dispatch, isolating a service, narrowing a
capability, switching to a known baseline, or requiring manual confirmation.

Containment may destroy evidence or worsen service if applied blindly. The
decision records expected benefit, cost, uncertainty, reversibility, and stop
condition. Incident urgency does not turn guesses into facts.

## Graceful Degradation Preserves the Important Contract

Graceful degradation is not “the system is slower.” It is an explicit move to
a smaller service envelope that preserves priority constraints while dropping
or narrowing less critical capability.

The degradation contract names protected functions, disabled functions,
capacity, quality and latency bounds, user-visible consequences, affected
groups, authority, monitoring, expiry, and recovery criteria. It should be
tested before the incident where possible.

For the package service, degradation might stop new releases, pin all clients
to the last independently observed safe package, disable cache promotion, and
serve a status notice. It should not silently continue vulnerable service
under a green control-plane label.

Different failures require different verbs. Fail-safe stops an action.
Fail-operational preserves essential service. Fail-soft reduces quality or
capacity. Fail-secure protects security properties. These goals can conflict.
Stopping a medical or infrastructure service may be more harmful than running
a constrained fallback. The architecture needs a consequence-specific choice,
not one universal “safe mode.”

Degradation can become permanent neglect. Every entry has an owner, budget,
review cadence, expiry, and exit condition. Users should know when service is
reduced and how to obtain remedy.

## Recovery, Compensation, and Closure

Recovery begins from an observed incident state, not from the state the plan
expected to exist. It chooses a target baseline, verifies required artifacts
and authority, performs bounded steps, observes each transition, and preserves
a fallback.

Restoration returns modeled state to a prior baseline. Reconstruction rebuilds
state from trusted artifacts. Replacement introduces a newly qualified
component. Compensation addresses effects that cannot be reversed. Remedy
addresses affected people and institutions. These routes can occur together.

The release incident may restore the old package pointer, remove the stale
cache objects, rebuild the patched artifact from verified source, redeploy
through a fresh lease, and independently inspect the served bytes. Users who
received the vulnerable package may need notification and mitigation. That
last obligation does not disappear when the service returns to green.

Closure requires evidence that the protected service envelope is restored or
that a legitimate authority accepted a narrower state; known residuals have
owners; affected parties received required communication and remedy; temporary
authority ended; and recurrence controls entered a tracked route.

Root-cause confidence is not required for containment, but causal claims at
closure should match the evidence. “Replication failure caused the incident”
may remain a hypothesis while the system accurately records which controls
failed and which repairs worked.

## Operations Must Survive the Governance Plane

The control system can fail during the incident it is meant to govern. The
artifact registry may be unavailable, the policy service partitioned, the
primary model degraded, the approval interface unreachable, or the audit store
suspect. A mature design cannot require perfect access to every governance
service before it can preserve essential safety and continuity.

Critical components need small offline contracts: last-known qualified
baselines, locally verifiable authority ceilings, emergency stop or isolation,
manual procedures, read-only artifact inventories, independent communication,
and reconstruction from protected records. Emergency action remains scoped and
later reconciled; offline capability is not a permanent bypass.

The recovery route should test loss of its own dependencies. Can operators
identify the exact running artifact without the central dashboard? Can they
revoke a credential when the orchestration service is down? Can essential
service continue without model access? Can the audit trail be rebuilt after a
collector fails? Can affected parties receive accurate communication through
an independent channel?

This produces two related availability goals. The governed service should
degrade safely when its workload dependencies fail. The governance plane
should itself degrade without granting broader authority or erasing evidence.
Availability cannot be purchased by failing open on consequential effects.

After recovery, learning enters through controlled changes. The incident may
revise detectors, inventories, runbooks, types, policies, proofs, tests, and
training. Each revision states which observed failure it addresses and which
claims remain unresolved. A successful response is not evidence that the new
control prevents recurrence until that control is independently exercised.

Incident metrics should preserve the denominator: detected and undetected
failures where known, false alarms, time to consequence recognition, time to
containment, service and human harm, residuals, recurrence, operator burden,
and repair completion. Rewarding only rapid closure encourages premature green
states.

## Unknown External Effects Remain Open

Open systems cannot enumerate every consumer or effect. An agent can publish
text that is copied, trigger a human decision, reveal a secret, change a market,
or cause another service to act. The artifact graph covers recorded edges; the
world contains unrecorded ones.

The system should represent an unknown external-effect residual when an action
crossed a boundary whose consequences are not fully observable. It can search
logs, query counterparties, inspect known consumers, and monitor indicators.
It cannot close the residual merely because no further evidence arrived.

This does not mean every action remains forever open. Policies define bounded
observation periods, materiality, escalation, notification, and archival
states. Closure can honestly say: known effects were restored, two external
copies were notified, and additional copies remain unobservable.

Such language is less satisfying than “rollback complete.” It is more useful
for future decisions.

## One End-to-End Operational Route

The corrected security release starts with a source snapshot and job contract.
The build produces a package whose graph binds source, dependency lock,
environment, tests, review, and exact bytes. An independent consumer checks
that required parents and non-claims are present.

The release adapter receives a proposal referencing that package. It checks
parent-job permission, release authority, approval scope, lease freshness,
target, impact, sandbox or service boundary, rollback inventory, secret
handles, and required observers. It captures pre-state and dispatches.

The control plane accepts the package. The receipt records this expected
partial result. A production probe then observes that one region serves the
old package. The joined route cannot declare success. It opens an incident,
halts further rollout, quarantines the stale region, and preserves essential
service through the last independently observed package.

Operators compare artifact lineage, replication logs, cache state, and served
bytes. They find a partial downstream failure. Recovery clears the affected
cache under a fresh lease, reapplies the release, and observes every region.
The artifact graph links the failed and repaired attempts. Temporary incident
authority expires. Residual users who may have received the old package remain
assigned to notification and remedy.

At no point does a log alone become reality. Logs propose event claims;
independent observations and bounded replays challenge them. At no point does
recovery erase history. The failed attempt remains available to explain why
the controls changed.

## Failure Cases

**Provenance theater.** Every object has a digest, but a decisive dependency or
configuration is outside the graph.

**Edge collapse.** “Related to” hides whether an artifact was built from,
reviewed against, deployed as, or merely linked to another.

**Log realism.** Collector records are treated as direct environmental truth.

**Shared-observer agreement.** Two green reports depend on one stale control-
plane source.

**Replay inflation.** Record or byte replay is presented as effect or
operational replay.

**Permission inheritance.** Tool access from a parent context becomes
authority for a different job or target.

**Approval drift.** A modified proposal executes under approval for an earlier
version.

**Revocation race.** A stale worker dispatches after authority changed.

**Secret materialization.** A credential enters model-visible context instead
of remaining behind a handle.

**No-mutation overclaim.** One denied call is treated as proof that no external
effect occurred.

**Receipt completion.** Command success substitutes for actual-state
observation.

**Rollback fiction.** The primary pointer is restored while caches, messages,
copies, or human consequences remain.

**Incident omniscience.** Response waits for certain root cause while harm
propagates.

**Unsafe safe mode.** A generic stop or fallback violates the service's most
important constraint.

**Permanent degradation.** Reduced service has no owner, expiry, remedy, or
funded exit.

**Green closure.** Service restoration erases affected-party obligations and
unknown external effects.

## The Strongest Simpler Baseline

The strongest baseline uses version control, reproducible builds, signed
artifacts, role-based access, established CI/CD, cloud audit logs, deployment
health checks, incident command, backups, runbooks, and post-incident review.
These systems already solve much of the practical problem and should be used
well before inventing a universal graph or adapter protocol.

The proposed architecture earns its cost when artifacts and effects cross many
tools, agents, organizations, and support decisions; when authority must remain
bound to parent work; when replay grades are routinely confused; or when
correction must propagate across technical and epistemic consumers.

Comparison should measure unauthorized attempts, provenance defects, time to
detect actual-state divergence, rollback completeness, residual discovery,
containment, service preservation, recurrence, human load, latency, and total
cost. Counts of nodes, receipts, logs, or incident fields are not outcomes.

If ordinary supply-chain and site-reliability practice produces equal
traceability, enforcement, observation, and recovery with less burden, the
architecture should consolidate around those practices.

## What the Current Work Establishes

The three technical owners have substantial but bounded executable artifacts.
Combining them here does not create deployment evidence or promote a core
claim.

Artifact Graphs has ten implemented public targets. The current proof surface
contains finite provenance, replay-grade, artifact-admission, replay-packet,
receipt-faithfulness, repository-audit, challenge, live-attestation, and
epistemic-trust-base predicates. The chapter records 56 live Lean theorem
declarations for the retained surface, with weaker declarations retired, plus
synthetic cross-record replay, receipt challenge, public artifact attestation,
and trust-base harnesses. These checks establish consequences over declared
records. They do not establish open-world provenance completeness, collector
truth, ACID storage, crash recovery, or external-effect atomicity.

Runtime Adapters has six implemented public targets and 68 Lean declarations
covering finite permission, approval, effect-lease, authority-ceiling,
confused-deputy, sandbox-escape, receipt, dispatch, replay, revocation, and
oversight-degradation routes. A public-safe probe performs one generated
temporary-file write and exact local restoration. Other deterministic probes
include two valid and twelve rejecting adversarial boundary cases, human-
oversight degradation records, and partitioned-authority fixtures. They do not
establish deployed sandbox enforcement, approval-service quality, secret-
handle safety, distributed revocation, policy correctness, reviewer
competence, or open-world rollback.

Governed Operations has three implemented targets through 26 Lean declarations
over finite degradation, recovery, and incident-lifecycle predicates. Current
executable work includes authored routing controls, eight real-subprocess
authority/effect/recovery cases, seven commit-bound service cases with crash
and restart behavior, localhost partition and outbox retry, stale-credential
and custody-tamper rejection, and a historical publication-service trace. The
claim-bearing natural-service campaign remains unexecuted. The results do not
establish detector quality, inventory completeness, natural incident-response
efficacy, safe degradation, deployed recovery, or transfer.

The repository therefore shows that selected record routes, rejection
conditions, local effects, and bounded recovery sequences can be implemented
and checked. It does not show that logs faithfully capture a hostile or open
world, that adapters contain capable agents in deployment, or that the joined
operations system improves real incidents.

## From a Minimum Effect Route to a Mature Operations Fabric

A minimum implementation can use the package release. Construct an artifact
graph from exact source, lockfile, build environment, package, tests, approval,
and release. Define the intended effect and complete inventory. Dispatch
through a scoped, expiring adapter lease. Observe the control plane and served
package independently. Inject the partial replication failure, require
degradation, execute recovery, and preserve one unknown external-effect
residual.

The next stage should compare this route with a strong conventional CI/CD and
incident process under prospectively frozen scenarios. Include stale grants,
approval mismatch, collector compromise, shared observers, partial writes,
crash and restart, network partition, secret exposure, rollback gaps, delayed
effects, and inaccessible consumers. Score real containment, service outcomes,
repair, and burden rather than record completion.

Natural campaigns need deployed services, independent ground truth where
available, red-team attempts, actual operators, complete incident denominators,
unknown-effect handling, and follow-up for recurrence. Artifact and adapter
claims should be reproduced across operating systems, infrastructures, tool
families, and organizations.

The mature operations fabric would connect every consequential proposal to a
bounded authority path, exact artifacts, observed effects, incident policy,
and recovery custody. It would support independent collectors and challenges,
graded replay, hardware-backed trust where warranted, distributed revocation,
and explicit residuals where the world cannot be closed.

It would degrade by preserving the service's most important contract rather
than merely stopping. It would treat affected-party remedy and external
copies as operational obligations. It would learn from incidents without
rewriting failed history or allowing successful recovery to promote unrelated
safety claims.

## The Strongest Objection

Artifact graphs, adapters, and incident packets can become an elaborate
simulation of control. Tools can escape mediation. Logs can omit effects.
Operators can rubber-stamp fields during an emergency. A larger control plane
can introduce new failure modes and make recovery dependent on the very system
that failed.

The objection is correct. A record layer is useful only where it is connected
to enforced boundaries, independent observation, tested recovery, competent
operators, and affected-party outcomes. More metadata can widen the attack
surface and delay urgent action.

The response is a small trusted base, consequence-scaled records, direct
testing of rejecting paths, offline and manual recovery, independent
observation, graceful operation when the governance service is unavailable,
and continuous comparison with ordinary operational practice. The system must
be able to explain which controls are declarative, simulated, enforced, and
observed.

No local proof can close the semantic and physical gap by itself. That gap is
managed through layered evidence and residual custody, not declared absent.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

The design should narrow if standard provenance, permissions, deployment
health checks, and incident practice achieve equal outcomes with lower
complexity. It should be rejected where the added machinery increases outage
duration, hides operator judgment, creates correlated control-plane failures,
or encourages false confidence.

Support would require prospective natural operations with independently
observed effects, adversarial attempts, complete costs, matched baselines,
actual recovery and compensation, reproduction, and transfer. The studies
should distinguish prevented dispatch from no effect, local restoration from
open-world reversal, and service recovery from affected-party remedy.

Artifact claims would strengthen if challenge audits detect planted omissions
and substitutions across heterogeneous collectors. Adapter claims would
strengthen if real sandboxes and services prevent confused-deputy, secret,
revocation, and escape attempts. Operations claims would strengthen if the
system detects divergence earlier, contains harm, preserves essential service,
and closes fewer incidents with hidden residuals.

## What This Establishes

Consequential work needs a trace from purpose and source to artifact, authority,
effect, observation, incident, recovery, and residual. Artifact edges need
roles. Logs are event claims. Replay has grades. Approval and effect leases are
scoped inputs. Command success is not actual-state truth. Rollback is a bounded
effect claim.

Governed operations begins when expected and observed state diverge. It assigns
command authority, contains propagation, chooses a consequence-specific
degradation envelope, recovers from observed state, compensates irreversible
effects, and preserves unknowns.

The current repository proves and executes selected finite parts of these
routes. It does not establish open-world faithfulness, deployed containment, or
incident efficacy.

One governed stack will eventually need to exchange procedures, artifacts, and
authority with another. Unit 18 moves from internal operations to protocol
semantics and inter-stack coordination.
